gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1016t:
Social Security Numbers, GAO-05-1016T of September 15, 2005, warns that a number made for one narrow job now opens doors across daily life. The Social Security Administration set the number in 1936 to track pay for benefits. Now firms and agencies use it to check who a person is. That wide use makes it a prime tool for identity theft.

The statement maps how public offices use the number. It maps use by some private firms too. It then lists the federal and state laws that curb use and punish theft of identity. Gaps in that shield remain, the title warns, and the text shows where they sit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1026t:
Ships' ballast water, and the pests it carries into U.S. waters, drive GAO-05-1026T, a statement of September 9, 2005. GAO counted at least 160 foreign water species set in the Great Lakes since the 1800s. A third came in the past 30 years, many via ballast. The zebra mussel alone cost an estimated $750 million to $1 billion from 1989 to 2000.

Federal steps to curb the flow date to 1990. New species still arrive, GAO notes. The statement walks through the laws and rules built so far. It then names the hard tests that still face the federal guard plan, from port checks to treatment gear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-326t:
Medicare Physician Payments, GAO-05-326T of February 10, 2005, lays out a fee rule that had begun to bite the doctors it pays. The sustainable growth rate plan ties yearly fee shifts to a growth cap. It cut fees by almost 5 percent in 2002. Later acts froze the cut for 2003, 2004, and 2005. Fresh cuts loom for 2006 to 2012.

GAO tells how the cap is meant to curb growth in doctor spend. It tells why fees still trend down in its math. It lays out ways to fix or swap the plan. Each way shifts what doctors earn and what Medicare spends.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-346t:
United Nations: Oil for Food Program Audits, GAO-05-346T of February 15, 2005, sums what inside audits found in a tainted aid plan. The plan, set in 1996, let Iraq sell oil to buy food, drugs, and works while bans held. Claims of fraud dog it. The old regime skimmed cash through smuggling and back-hand fees on deals. A free probe team formed in April 2004.

In January 2005, that team put out 58 inside audit reports. GAO tells who ran those audits and with what staff and cash. It lifts their chief finds. It marks where the audits could not reach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-416t:
Internal Revenue Service, GAO-05-416T of April 14, 2005, weighs the tax arm's fiscal year 2006 cash ask next to its early 2005 form. The arm shifts weight from help for filers to hunt for cheats. It takes its vast tech build in house from hired firms. Both shifts hold sense, GAO notes, and both hold risk. A short purse forces the trade in the first place.

GAO asks how the ask splits cash between help and hunt, and what filers will feel. It asks how the tech build fares. It asks if the arm's tech run costs rest on best craft. It grades the tax rush just past.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-436t:
Air Force contracts tainted by a biased official are the matter in testimony GAO-05-436T, presented on April 14, 2005. Darlene Druyun, a former senior Air Force procurement official, had admitted bias in favor of The Boeing Company. She was later convicted of breaking a post-employment law. Rival firms protested awards for the small diameter bomb and the C-130 avionics upgrade. GAO heard the protests under the Competition in Contracting Act of 1984.

Federal rules require government business to be run with full fairness and no favored treatment. GAO sustained the protests on both programs. The Air Force had not shown that the bias did not harm the protesters. In the C-130 case, Druyun had led the procurement throughout. GAO also found that evaluators had been told to destroy parts of the record. Talks with offerors had not been fair or complete. The testimony explains why the awards could not stand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-466t:
Two cargo security programs run by Customs and Border Protection are summed up in testimony GAO-05-466T, dated May 26, 2005. The Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism gives firms faster treatment when they tighten shipment security. The Container Security Initiative aims to screen high-risk containers at foreign ports before they sail.

Firms in the partnership gain benefits before the agency checks that their security steps are real. The agency's goal was to check members within 3 years, but it had checked only 11 percent of them. Those checks were also weak. Their scope was set jointly with the firm checked, and no written rules set how deep a check should go. The program lacked a full set of performance measures. The container program had improved sharing between U.S. and foreign customs staff. GAO said both programs needed tighter management to work as planned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-476t:
Support for GAO's fiscal year 2006 budget request is offered in testimony GAO-05-476T, presented on April 19, 2005. The statement says the funds are needed so GAO can help Congress meet its constitutional duties. It also ties the request to better performance and accountability across the federal government. GAO thanks Congress for past support and argues that money put into its work pays back far more.

The years ahead will press hard on federal finances, the statement warns. The current deficit and the long-term fiscal imbalance will force tough choices. Lawmakers must decide what government should do, how it should work, and how it should be paid for. GAO points to its 21st Century Challenges report as a guide for that rethink. It links GAO's own needs to the wider fiscal debate then facing Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-516t:
Fire safety, building work, and money handling at the Kennedy Center come under review in testimony GAO-05-516T, presented on April 6, 2005. The center had received nearly $203 million in federal funds since fiscal year 1995 for capital projects. It planned to seek $43 million more through fiscal year 2008. Its building plan ties the work to renovation, life safety, and access for people with disabilities.

GAO examined how far key projects had come and whether they stayed within cost estimates. It also checked what the center told stakeholders about that progress. A second thread covered plans to meet fire safety and disabled access rules. GAO urged the board chairman to increase oversight and to comply better with fire code. The center agreed that more oversight would help. It held that it already met fire code but agreed to seek an outside review of some weak points. The testimony presses for tighter control.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-546t:
Which fiscal laws bind the E-rate fund is the question in testimony GAO-05-546T, presented on April 11, 2005. The Federal Communications Commission's program had committed more than $13 billion since 1998 to connect schools and libraries. GAO's February 2005 report found the program housed in an unusual private setup. This testimony focuses on the Antideficiency Act, the law that bars spending beyond available funds.

GAO agreed with the commission on the core point. The Universal Service Fund counts as a permanent, open-ended appropriation. It is bound by the Antideficiency Act. Letters that promise E-rate funding count as obligations under the act. GAO suggested Congress weigh a break from the act, lasting 2 or 3 years. A narrower break could let the commission count some expected receipts as resources. Such a pause would let a study of the fund finish. Then Congress could settle which rules should govern the program for good.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-576t:
Oversight of the housing finance giants is the issue in testimony GAO-05-576T, presented on April 21, 2005. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Home Loan Bank System held combined obligations of $4.6 trillion at the end of 2003. Freddie Mac admitted accounting faults in 2003. Fannie Mae was cited in 2004 for accounting faults and earnings manipulation. GAO laid out the firms' missions and risks and the case for a new regulator.

Taxpayers could face the bill if one failed, and markets could shake. The watch over them is split and weak. One office guards Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and a separate board guards the home loan banks. The first office lacks key legal powers a regulator needs. The housing department, which watches the two firms' mission work, lacks staff and funds for the job.  GAO argued the oversight frame must be rebuilt to match.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-586t:
A growing backlog of forest land that needs replanting is the subject of testimony GAO-05-586T, presented on April 27, 2005. In 2004 the Forest Service told Congress nearly 900,000 acres needed reforestation. Thinning and clearing rival plants follow, to help young stands thrive. The testimony draws on a GAO report issued the same day. It asks how the need has grown, what drives it, and what harm may follow.

Land needing treatment has risen since 2000, the data suggest. The figures are firm enough to show the trend, but not to set exact needs or budgets. Regions define their needs in unlike ways, and records are not kept current. Fire, insects, and disease now drive most new need, not logging.  Funding for damage from natural causes has stayed flat while the need climbs.  A new data system is coming, GAO said, but alone it will not fix the numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-616t:
New hiring and pay freedoms for agencies fill this testimony, GAO-05-616T of April 21, 2005. Congress has already freed over 1.2 million federal workers from parts of the old personnel rules. GAO says freedoms pay off only with committed leaders and solid groundwork: planning tied to mission, skill to build new systems, and fair reviews of staff performance. Agencies use the tools unevenly so far.

GAO's own reform path offers a model. It urges Congress to make agencies prove the groundwork exists before granting more freedom. One test already bites: higher executive pay requires a review system that truly separates strong staff from weak.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-706t:
Social Security's shield for the vulnerable is weighed in GAO testimony GAO-05-706T (May 17, 2005). Before 1935 at least half of older Americans depended on kin or charity. Today old-age poverty runs below the national rate. The shield's parts: a formula favoring low-wage workers, disability cover, spouse and survivor benefits, and a yearly cost-of-living raise. Society has moved since: longer lives, more women at work, new household shapes, slower workforce growth.

Those shifts strain the design. GAO airs open questions on spousal fairness, work incentives for older staff, and disability rules, all under a solvency cloud.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-786t:
Social Security and public workers meet in testimony GAO-05-786T, presented June 9, 2005. The program covers about 96 percent of U.S. workers. Most of the rest work for state, local, or federal bodies. They do not pay the tax on their public pay. Yet many can still draw benefits. A House panel asked GAO to explain the fairness issues and the reform stakes.

GAO said about one-fourth of public workers sit outside the system. Two rules cut benefits for those with outside pensions. One hits spouse and survivor benefits. The other hits worker benefits. But data on many state and local pensions is missing. So the rules are not applied in an even way. Critics call them confusing and unfair, GAO noted. Reform plans would revise or scrap them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-836t:
Medicaid maximization by states is revisited in testimony GAO-05-836T, given June 28, 2005. The program covers almost 54 million people. It cost $276 billion in fiscal year 2003. GAO placed it on the high-risk list in 2003. States have found many ways to draw more federal money. Some pay consultants only when reimbursements rise. The testimony draws on a report issued the same day.

GAO described three strands of the problem. Some states raised federal payments in improper ways. School-based services and admin costs were one channel for growth. Contingency-fee consultants were another. The federal Medicaid agency's oversight of these efforts is the third strand. The testimony's verdict matches the report behind it. Stronger federal oversight is needed to guard the program's fiscal integrity.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-896t:
Checked baggage screening gear is tracked in testimony GAO-05-896T, given July 13, 2005. Law required all checked bags to be screened by machines by December 31, 2003. Two machine types were rushed to over 400 airports. GAO covered the rollout and its effects. It checked moves to build machines into conveyor lines. And it weighed steps to place gear in the best way.

GAO found much progress on coverage. But early machines stood alone in lobbies, not in line with conveyors. That setup needs more screeners and slows work. Eighty-six of 130 airports GAO surveyed have, plan, or weigh in-line systems. Total costs are unknown, and future federal funding is uncertain. Better planning is needed to place the systems well, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1006t:
Defense business overhaul and steady leadership frame testimony GAO-06-1006T, delivered August 3, 2006. The Defense Department bears sole charge of eight high-risk areas. It shares six more government-wide areas. Weaknesses cut across all its major business work. Billions of dollars are wasted each year, GAO says, through weak performance and poor accountability.

The testimony walks through the long-standing flaws and their cost to efficiency. It gives cases that show why oversight of business systems must improve. It lists the department's key drives to fix financial management and the systems behind it. It closes with actions needed to raise the odds that the overhaul succeeds. The title names the core need: sustained leadership at the top.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1086t:
Guardianships for older people who cannot manage their own affairs are the theme of GAO-06-1086T, testimony presented in September 2006. The Senate Special Committee on Aging asked GAO to follow up its 2004 report. Courts appoint guardians to act for incapacitated elderly people. The earlier work asked how well courts ensure guardians do their duties. GAO spoke with lawyers, agency officials, and staff at courts praised earlier.

The testimony reports little progress since 2004. GAO had urged the Social Security Administration to convene a joint study group on payee programs. Other agencies said they would take part, but SSA disagreed. Its stance had not changed. A second call asked the Department of Health and Human Services to back state pilot efforts. That work also moved slowly. The statement serves readers who track elder protection and benefit safeguards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1096t:
Emergency planning for the capital region is assessed in GAO-06-1096T, testimony presented on September 28, 2006. The National Capital Region partners had just approved a homeland security strategic plan that month. GAO had urged such a plan in a May 2004 report and June 2004 testimony. It checked the region's planning again in July 2005 and March 2006. A Senate panel now asked GAO to judge the finished plan.

GAO weighed the plan against traits that strong strategic plans share. It asked whether goals and priorities for readiness were clear. It also asked how well the plan lets partners track progress toward those goals. The testimony notes ways the plan's substance could grow stronger at its next review. The region's coordination office must align many federal, state, and local actors. A shared plan gives that crowded field one set of targets.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1116t:
Pay for top federal leaders and judges is the subject of GAO-06-1116T, testimony presented on September 20, 2006. The statement draws on GAO's recent report on executive and judicial pay, GAO-06-708. Government reform, GAO notes, starts with leadership. Yet the way the government classifies, pays, and motivates its senior people has changed little for decades. That gap is sharpest at the very top, among senior executives and federal judges.

The testimony lays out recent trends in what these leaders earn. It compares their pay paths with broader workforce and cost trends. The pattern, GAO found, points to a need to rethink the full compensation package, not just salaries. Benefits, pay caps, and compression all shape whether the government can draw strong leaders. The statement gives Congress a factual base for that debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1126t:
Two climate topics share GAO-06-1126T, testimony presented on September 27, 2006. The first is the clarity of federal climate funding reports, drawn from GAO's August 2005 study. The second covers two voluntary programs, from an April 2006 report. The Environmental Protection Agency runs Climate Leaders, and the Department of Energy runs Climate VISION. Both seek cuts in greenhouse gas emissions through voluntary industry action.

On funding, GAO found reports that shifted form and method without clear notes, which blocked fair comparisons. It urged steady formats, plain explanations of changes, and data on climate tax breaks. The budget and science offices agreed with most of that advice. On the voluntary side, GAO judged the two programs' progress and what held them back. It pressed both agencies to do more to spur real gains. The testimony joins budget honesty with program results in one climate review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-136t:
Costly leasing of federal office space is flagged in GAO-06-136T, testimony presented on October 6, 2005. GAO placed federal real property on its high-risk list in January 2003. Heavy reliance on leased space was a main reason. The government owns and leases about 3.3 billion square feet in roughly half a million buildings. Over 380 million square feet are leased. Buying or building usually costs less over time than operating leases.

Budget rules help explain the habit. Ownership costs land in the budget all at once, in full. Lease costs can spread across years, so leases look cheaper in any single year. The General Services Administration lacks funds for ownership, so it leases even for long-term needs. One patent office lease was set to cost $48 million more than construction. GAO found the core problems unchanged since 2003. Repair backlogs alone run to tens of billions of dollars.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-216t:
NASA's broken financial systems are the subject of GAO-06-216T, testimony presented on October 27, 2005. The space agency has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1990. Weak contract oversight is a core reason, fed by poor data on contract spending. GAO laid out the agency's chief money problems. It compared them with peer agencies and graded progress on past advice. A companion report, issued the same day, urged one master schedule for the fix.

The new core financial system failed to cure the worst flaws, GAO found. It cannot support key balances with transaction-level records. It posts entries to the wrong accounts and hides corrections. The agency automated its old, weak habits instead of changing them. It also starved the work of skilled financial staff. Most agencies now earn clean audit opinions; NASA's books remain unauditable. GAO said strong leadership must drive the overhaul.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-226t:
United Nations oversight and buying habits get early scrutiny in GAO-06-226T, testimony dated October 31, 2005. The Oil for Food scandal revived old doubts about how the UN watches itself. An independent inquiry had just reported on that program's abuses. The UN's 2005 World Summit also called for broad management reform. GAO shared early findings from two studies still under way. One covers the UN's internal oversight office; the other covers its procurement system.

The testimony asks whether the oversight office can act freely and well. Its budget path runs through the very body it must audit, which can cramp its reach. GAO also weighed UN efforts to make buying more open and professional. Reports with fuller findings were due early the next year. The statement gives Congress a first read on reform pressure at the UN. It frames the questions that deeper audits would answer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-246t:
Early findings on hurricane relief contracts arrive in GAO-06-246T, testimony presented on November 8, 2005. Weeks after Katrina and Rita hit the Gulf Coast, Congress wanted a first account of the buying behind the rescue. GAO had begun to review how agencies hired firms for debris, housing, and repair work. Much of that buying moved at emergency speed, with little competition. This statement reports what the reviewers had learned so far.

First signs matched a known pattern. When disaster deals are struck in days, prices and terms get thin scrutiny. Past storms had already shown how no-bid awards invite waste. GAO said its teams would track contract files, costs, and oversight across the relief effort. The point of speaking early was to mark risks while the money still flowed. Congress could then press agencies to tighten controls before the largest recovery sums were spent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-266t:
How well the flight safety system grades itself is the question in GAO-06-266T, testimony dated November 17, 2005. U.S. commercial flying has a superb safety record, yet rare crashes carry tragic weight. The Federal Aviation Administration aims its programs at the highest risks. It trains inspectors to apply the rules in a steady way. This statement, built from recent GAO reports, tests each of those three legs.

The system works, GAO said, but its gains are not fully cashed in. Risk-based airline checks still share the stage with older, blanket inspection habits. Outside designees do about 90 percent of certification work, yet the agency lacked clear tests for judging that program. Its enforcement database holds gaps that blunt analysis. Training mostly follows sound practice, though system safety skills need more depth. GAO's advice: judge each program by results, with data fit for the task.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-346t:
A national plan for electronic health records, still taking shape, is tracked in GAO-06-346T, testimony given March 15, 2006. Digital records could lift the quality and speed of care. In April 2004 the president called for records that work across systems within ten years. A national coordinator post was created that spring. A framework for action followed two months later. In May 2005 GAO urged the health department to set detailed plans and milestones. The department agreed. This statement grades progress since then.

The department is continuing its efforts, GAO said, in careful phrasing. A strategy is being defined rather than executed. The statement also surveys health technology work across federal agencies. Public health data sharing features in the wider record. In an emergency, linked systems could speed the response. The testimony measures a long campaign at its start. Its caution: frameworks do not treat patients; working systems do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-406t:
The whole federal government's books still could not earn a clean verdict. Testimony GAO-06-406T, dated March 1, 2006, covers the fiscal year 2005 U.S. government financial statements. Law requires GAO to audit those combined statements each year. Congress and the President need timely and reliable figures to steer programs and policy.

GAO warns that the audit problems carry real costs. They hamper reliable reporting of assets, debts, and costs. They make the full cost of some programs hard to measure. They also weaken care of assets and records. GAO urges sustained gains in financial management. The statement links bookkeeping to the nation's long-term fiscal imbalance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-456t:
Entitlement spending sits at the heart of the nation's long-term budget strain. Testimony GAO-06-456T, given February 15, 2006, discusses mandatory spending and fiscal challenges. It draws on a GAO report on reexamining the base of the federal government. That report posed questions for policy makers across the budget. Areas include discretionary spending, mandatory spending, and tax policy.

GAO says meeting long-term challenges must include a fresh look at mandatory programs. Committees can use the questions to pick areas that need attention. The statement gives examples of hard choices the nation faces. Readers get a framework, not a single bill. The focus stays on trade-offs across government.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-526t:
Airwaves are scarce, and demand for wireless service keeps climbing. The testimony numbered GAO-06-526T, delivered March 14, 2006, covers options and barriers for spectrum reform. The radio-frequency spectrum carries services vital to the economy and to missions such as national security. Most usable spectrum is already assigned to current users. Concern grows that the management system cannot meet future demand. The testimony rests on earlier GAO reports.

GAO reports how far market-based methods have spread for commercial users. It gives the same measure for federal users. It then sets out options to improve spectrum management. It also names barriers to reform. Readers get a concise map of a technical policy fight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-586t:
A number created to track earnings became the key to identity theft. Delivered March 30, 2006, testimony GAO-06-586T covers protection of Social Security numbers. The Social Security Administration created the number in 1936 to track workers' earnings. It has since become the identifier of choice for public and private bodies. Thieves seek it to build false identities for financial misuse. Congress and some states have moved to limit its use and display.

GAO draws on its past reports and testimonies. It describes how agencies and some private firms use the number. It reviews federal laws that govern its use and disclosure. Gaps remain, and more could be done, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-606t:
In GAO-06-606T, testimony dated April 26, 2006, GAO shared its views on plans to reshape the United States nuclear weapons complex. The National Nuclear Security Administration runs three design labs, four production plants, and the Nevada Test Site. A task force review in October 2005 set out a vision for the complex over the next 25 years.

GAO said the agency had steps under way, such as a design contest for the Reliable Replacement Warhead. It had also sought over $15 million more to dismantle old weapons. But GAO warned that clear long-term needs, sound cost estimates, and a firm plan were still key. The testimony shows how hard it is to shrink an aging complex and keep it safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-626t:
Military space programs and their cost problems are covered in GAO-06-626T, testimony dated April 6, 2006. For decades, defense space projects have cost hundreds of millions, even billions, more than planned. Schedules have slipped by years, and performance risks have grown. GAO was asked to sum up its past findings on why space buying goes wrong. GAO also set out the steps needed to get better results.

GAO told the Senate panel that programs often start with shaky cost estimates and unproven technology. That pattern locks in overruns before hardware is built. GAO pointed to proven practices, such as matching needs to resources early. The testimony gives lawmakers a clear guide to the fixes that matter most.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-696t:
Jobless benefits and their weak points fill GAO-06-696T, testimony presented on May 4, 2006. Unemployment Insurance has backed the income security of the workforce for over 70 years. In fiscal year 2004, it covered about 129 million workers and paid about $41 billion to nearly 9 million job losers. The Labor Department and the states share the duty to run the program well.

GAO reported that about $3.4 billion in benefits was overpaid nationwide in calendar year 2004. The Labor Department blamed a majority of overpayments on improper actions by claimants. States and employers also played a part. The department had launched steps to help states detect and prevent bad payments. GAO also stressed services that help claimants return to work sooner.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-746t:
Where the disaster agency should sit in government is debated in GAO-06-746T, testimony GAO gave on May 9, 2006. Hurricane Katrina had raised hard questions about national readiness for catastrophic events. Some lawmakers wanted to pull the Federal Emergency Management Agency out of the Homeland Security Department. GAO offered factors for future success and points to weigh on placement. The testimony drew on GAO's wide body of Katrina work.

GAO said the agency's troubles would not be fixed simply by making it independent. Many lessons from Katrina were applied during Hurricane Rita, with a much better response. That record suggested that placement was not the main key to success. GAO urged leaders to fix operational weaknesses first, wherever the agency sits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-756t:
Anthrax defenses get a status report in GAO-06-756T, testimony GAO gave on May 9, 2006. GAO had studied anthrax vaccine safety and detection methods for the past seven years. After the 2001 attacks, agencies lacked validated ways to test for contamination in buildings. GAO had urged a coordinated approach with probability-based sampling. GAO also tracked work on a next-generation anthrax vaccine to replace the current one.

GAO reported that agencies had taken some steps to validate sampling methods. For the 2001 incidents, responders used targeted sampling based on their best judgment at the time. GAO explained when sampling method matters most and when it matters less. Progress on the new vaccine was also under way. The testimony measures slow gains in a key biodefense area.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-866t:
Veteran data security after a major breach fills GAO-06-866T, testimony GAO gave on June 14, 2006. A theft had just compromised personal data on millions of veterans held by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The breach threw a harsh light on the department's long-known security weaknesses. GAO and the department's inspector general had reported them for years. GAO summed up what leadership must now do.

GAO found recurring weaknesses across the department's systems. Access controls, physical security, and separation of duties all had gaps. The department lacked a robust information security program to hold the pieces together. That lack, GAO said, is what lets sensitive data be compromised. GAO called for leadership to address both security and privacy with urgency. The testimony is a post-breach reckoning for a troubled program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-886t:
Safe operation of the nation's 103 commercial nuclear power plants is the charge of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, or NRC. GAO gave early views on NRC oversight in testimony GAO-06-886T, dated June 15, 2006. In 2000 NRC had launched a new Reactor Oversight Process to fix a system seen as loose and uneven.

GAO told how NRC watches plants and what five years of the new process showed. It used program-wide data, inspection results, and close study of 11 plants. The testimony flags parts of the process that still need work. It also tracks NRC steps already under way to improve them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-896t:
Sharing the cost of fighting wildland fires is the question in GAO testimony GAO-06-896T, dated June 21, 2006. Fires often burn both federal and nonfederal land, plus homes near wildlands. Deals between the levels of government set how crews work together and split costs.

The testimony builds on GAO's May 2006 report, GAO-06-570. GAO reviewed how costs are split when fires cross those lines. It also gathered worries about the current framework. GAO urged clearer guidance on which split method fits which fire, and on who owes what. The record shows why vague rules strain joint fire work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-976t:
Fake papers at land borders are tested again in GAO testimony GAO-06-976T, dated August 2, 2006. U.S. citizens did not then need a passport to enter from lands in the Western Hemisphere. They had to prove citizenship to an officer's liking, with papers such as birth records and photo ID.

In 2003 GAO agents entered from Canada and Mexico with false names and fake papers. Later tries mostly worked too, though one entry was refused. Congress asked if the flaw still stood. GAO ran a fresh probe to find out. The testimony reports lasting weakness in screening entrants, a risk it says terrorists could exploit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1016t:
Tree cutting and clearing projects cleared without full environmental study are counted in GAO testimony GAO-07-1016T, dated June 28, 2007. The Forest Service tends over 192 million acres. Big projects need an environmental study first. Small classes of work, found harmless in advance, can skip that step.

From 2003 the agency held one such class for plant work, then added four more. GAO told how many projects were cleared in calendar years 2003 through 2005, and which classes were used. It asked why some field offices shun the fast path. The work polled all 155 national forests, and rests on GAO report GAO-07-99.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1106t:
Groundwork for the 2010 Census is under way, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1106T, dated July 17, 2007. The count, set by the Constitution, splits House seats, redraws districts, and guides billions in federal aid. The Census Bureau puts the 2010 cost at $11.3 billion, the most costly count ever after price growth.

GAO asked if the bureau has a full project plan with fresh cost data. It checked use of lessons from dress rehearsal work. It weighed how tech for the new count is run. It asked if plans cover zones hit by Hurricanes Katrina and Rita. Steady watch and risk care stay vital, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1246t:
The Department of Veterans Affairs runs its hospitals and benefits on technology systems. In GAO-07-1246T, dated September 19, 2007, GAO reviewed the department's push to centralize control of those systems. The department spends about $1 billion a year on technology. Its realignment began in October 2005 and was due to finish by July 2008. GAO drew on its recent reports on the effort.

GAO found real progress toward the new structure by May 2007. Still, the plan skipped one key success factor: a team dedicated to managing the change. New management processes were also slow to spread. Only 2 of 36 planned processes had reached pilot testing by May 2007. GAO flagged weak controls over technology equipment at four audited sites. It also noted split duties for information security with no set way to coordinate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1256t:
Reports of poor outpatient care at Walter Reed Army Medical Center shocked the public in February 2007. GAO gave early observations on the response in GAO-07-1256T on September 26, 2007. The Army had acted on its own service's problems first. A joint Defense and Veterans Affairs committee took on the wider system issues. GAO reviewed case management, disability ratings, brain injury and stress care, and data sharing.

The Army built Warrior Transition Units to guide wounded troops through care, GAO noted. Each soldier gets a team of three key staff inside the unit. Still, GAO saw hard problems in all four areas it reviewed. Disability decisions had long been slow and uneven across the services. The two departments also struggled to share health data smoothly. GAO said lasting fixes would need steady oversight and enough resources.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-196t:
A company can be formed in the United States without naming who owns it. GAO explained the risk in testimony GAO-07-196T on November 14, 2006. The statement draws on GAO's April 2006 report on company formations. Shell companies can hide crimes such as money laundering. GAO surveyed all 50 states and the District of Columbia. It also reviewed state laws and spoke with police and industry officials.

Most states collect no ownership data when a company forms, GAO found. They also skip it in yearly reports. Firms that file the paperwork for others gather only billing details. In 2004, some 869,693 corporations and 1,068,989 limited liability companies were formed. Police told GAO that hidden ownership slows their cases. Other sources, like bank and tax records, can help but are hard to use. The testimony weighs the cost of collecting more data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-266t:
Medicare pays dialysis clinics one bundled rate for routine care but pays extra for key drugs. GAO argued for one full bundle in testimony GAO-07-266T on December 6, 2006. The statement draws on GAO's report on kidney failure care. The bundled rate dates to 1983 and skips inflation updates. It now covers less of routine care's true cost. Drugs billed apart are paid at average sales price plus 6 percent since 2006.

Paying for drugs apart rewards heavier drug use, the testimony says. Clinics gain when they bill more units of costly drugs. A single rate for all services would end that pull. It would also let clinics choose treatments more freely. The Medicare agency studied a full bundle in 2003 and found it feasible. Congress required that study of expanded bundling. GAO's report urged lawmakers to direct the change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-386t:
Over $130 billion flowed to homeland security after 2001, with risk logic applied unevenly. GAO surveyed the pattern in testimony GAO-07-386T on February 7, 2007. The statement sums up earlier GAO work. It covers grant formulas, transport and port programs, and department strategy. Risk management means weighing threat, weakness, and impact. GAO asked where that weighing guides the money.

The Coast Guard leads the department on risk method, GAO said. Its assessments still lack full reliability. The aviation agency's risk work has gaps. It had set no method or schedule for rating air cargo weaknesses. General aviation never got a systematic threat review. Grant decisions did not always follow risk scores. The department lacks one risk-based strategic plan. GAO urged applying the principles at every level. Prior reports carry the detailed fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-426t:
Iraq rebuilding stalls under strain from three sides, and GAO testimony GAO-07-426T, given February 15, 2007, lays out each one. The Defense Department leaned hard on contractors for big projects and for support to troops in the field. Results often fell short. At the same time, Iraq's government had to cut violence and keep basic services running.

The statement first asks what shapes contract results in Iraq. It then turns to the worsening security picture and the state of Iraqi forces. Last, it weighs whether Iraq's government can sustain gains on its own. The testimony rests on years of GAO work on rebuilding, contracting, and troop support. It gives Congress a frank view of why progress lagged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-436t:
Hard times in the Northern Mariana Islands fill GAO testimony GAO-07-436T, presented February 8, 2007. The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is a self-governing U.S. area of 14 islands in the North Pacific. The testimony draws on a December 2006 GAO report on four insular areas. A Senate committee chair asked GAO to present the CNMI results.

CNMI's economy rests on two industries, which leaves it exposed. Its books were late and patchy, so leaders lacked sound facts for choices. Weak internal controls raised the risk of fraud and waste. Federal help, through training and funds, had brought slow and uneven gains. GAO warned that the fiscal squeeze would deepen without better records. The statement frames what Congress can watch as aid continues.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-446t:
The Coast Guard's Deepwater fleet renewal draws early warnings in GAO testimony GAO-07-446T, presented February 15, 2007. Deepwater was meant to replace aging cutters and aircraft. After the September 11 attacks, the plan grew to fit new security missions. Past GAO work faulted the service for weak watch over its system integrator.

The testimony rests on audit work from August 2006 to February 2007. It reviews the troubled plan to stretch 110-foot patrol boats to 123 feet. That stopgap ran into hull and cost problems. It then grades the wider buying effort and the service's grip on cost and contractors. GAO saw progress in planning but gaps in control. The statement gives Congress an early read before more funds flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-556t:
People problems head the federal risk list in GAO testimony GAO-07-556T, presented March 6, 2007. Long fiscal strain, an aging workforce, and new ways of governing press every agency at once. GAO keeps strategic human capital management on its high-risk list. The testimony rests on years of GAO work across the government.

Agencies, it finds, often lack modern hiring, training, and reward systems. Reform plans exist, but follow-through is patchy. The Office of Personnel Management must also build the muscle to lead change government-wide. Skills gaps in fields like contracting and cyber work recur. GAO frames workforce skill as the hinge of every other reform. Systems and budgets matter, the statement holds, but no transformation outruns the staff who must run it. Lawmakers are urged to treat hiring law as core policy, not back-office detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-566t:
Air tankers and cargo planes age while replacements stall, and GAO testimony GAO-07-566T, delivered March 7, 2007, urges care before big buys. The Defense Department is spending billions to upgrade C-5 and C-130 fleets and to buy a new tanker. Weapons buying has been a GAO high-risk area since 1990. Sound buys need firm needs, proven tech, honest cost math, and full funding. Those parts keep going missing.

The statement first probes the studies behind air mobility needs. It questions the analysis for the KC-X tanker in sharp terms. It then lists what must change for better results across weapons work. GAO suggests Congress ask for a formal pledge that the tanker needs were set by a sound, traceable process. Tight budgets, it warns, no longer absorb the old pattern of cost growth and delay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-576t:
Voting machines need guarding at every level of government, and GAO testimony GAO-07-576T, delivered March 7, 2007, lays out the shared task. Doubts after the 2000 election pushed Congress to act. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 paid to swap old gear for electronic systems. It set up the Election Assistance Commission to lead reform. GAO's reports helped frame that law.

Later GAO work flagged security and reliability flaws in the new systems. The testimony first sets out what these machines do in a count. It then lists the flaws reported by states and experts. State and local practice comes next, drawn from surveys on the 2004 and 2006 votes. The close looks ahead: paper trails, testing, and staff skill all need work. No single level of government, GAO holds, can secure the ballot alone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-596t:
Early word on how the Pentagon runs its spy asset queue fills GAO testimony GAO-07-596T, delivered April 19, 2007. Wartime demand for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) data keeps outgrowing supply. The 2006 Quadrennial Defense Review told the ISR world to integrate better. Big buys of new systems are planned at the same time. Congress asked how the department juggles old fleets and new ones.

The remarks are early findings from live work. GAO read program files, met officials, watched U.S. Central Command work, and reviewed 12 airborne ISR programs in build. Three strands emerge. First, the status of reforms meant to unify how needs get set. Next, how today's assets get tasked for live missions. Last, whether new programs in build overlap each other. The early read: reform plans exist, but the services still guard their own fleets first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-606t:
Three days after a twin statement to another panel, GAO repeated its wounded-troops brief in testimony GAO-07-606T, dated March 8, 2007. The count of the war-wounded stood above 24,000 as of March 1, 2007. The source work spans GAO reports from 2004 through 2006. Two vast systems share the caseload: military hospitals first, veterans' hospitals after.

Rather than fresh field work, this version restates the four trouble spots for a new room. Care transfers between the systems lead. Speed of first rehab for the worst hurt follows. The third strand asks who screens for post-traumatic stress disorder, and whether veterans' clinics can absorb the need. Pay errors that drain family budgets close the brief. The repeat itself is a signal: the same four seams were still splitting in 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-616t:
Food aid buys less food each year though budgets hold, and GAO testimony GAO-07-616T, presented March 21, 2007, explains the math. The United States gives over half the world's food aid. Since the 2002 farm bill renewal, Congress has given an average of $2 billion a year. Ships moved an average of 4 million metric tons a year. Yet loads fell 43 percent over 5 years.

Rising shipping and business costs eat the difference. For the biggest program, such costs take about 65 percent of all spending. With the 2007 farm bill in draft, GAO sorted the drags on delivery. Weak joint planning among agencies and shippers wastes time. Thin checks at the far end leave aid's fate unsure. The testimony urges tighter logistics and real monitoring, so each dollar lands as meals, not freight bills.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-626t:
Guarding the nation's core systems is slow, joint work, and GAO testimony GAO-07-626T, presented March 20, 2007, reports the pace. About 85 percent of critical infrastructure sits in private hands. Power grids, banks, water plants, and data networks all count. The Department of Homeland Security leads a national plan built on councils for each sector. Hurricane Katrina showed how fast these systems can fail together.

The testimony leans on an October 2006 GAO report on the councils. It tracks how many councils stand formed. It lists what helps or hinders their birth and their sector plans. Cyber defense duties get a status check as well. Plans lag the plan's own dates in many sectors. Past GAO advice on cyber work sits half-done. The statement holds that the council model can work, but trust and data sharing between firms and the state remain the weak seams.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-636t:
A billion flyers a year by 2015 will not fit today's air system, and GAO testimony GAO-07-636T, given March 22, 2007, centers on the rebuild. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) runs one of the safest systems in the world. Growth is outrunning it. The Next Generation Air Transportation System, or NextGen, is the planned redesign. A charter renewal fight gave Congress a chance to probe the plan.

Three topics fill the statement. The first grades early FAA steps that could lay NextGen's base, such as new navigation methods. The second lists what must be settled for the shift to succeed, from funding to workforce skills. The third turns to safety in the system as it stands and as it will stand. GAO draws on recent reports and live studies. The warning is plain: a redesign this size fails on management long before it fails on technology.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-646t:
Testing students who are still learning English is the hard case in GAO testimony GAO-07-646T, delivered March 23, 2007. The No Child Left Behind Act of 2001 put over 5 million such students under yearly progress goals. A test given in a language a child half-knows may measure the language, not the learning. The testimony rests on a July 2006 GAO report, GAO-06-815.

GAO studied five states in depth: California, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina, and Texas. It asked how far these students hit the goals. It checked what states do to make both subject tests and English tests fair. It then graded the Education Department's help to states. Gains exist, but valid scores for this group remain the weak joint of the whole law. The statement urges more federal aid aimed at test design for these students.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-656t:
Two engines for one fighter jet: GAO testimony GAO-07-656T, presented March 22, 2007, prices the rivalry. The Joint Strike Fighter will replace hundreds of aircraft across three services. Since 1996, the Defense Department has funded a second, alternate engine to compete with the main one. Backers claim rivalry saves money and lifts quality. Section 211 of a fiscal year 2007 defense law told GAO to run the cost math.

GAO modeled sole-source and head-to-head paths for design, production, and upkeep of the engine. It mined past engine programs for what rivalry in fact delivered. It then weighed what killing the alternate engine would do to the supplier base. The department offered no comments on the findings. The statement is a cost ledger for a live budget fight: the second engine costs money now, on a bet that rivalry pays it back over decades of production.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-746t:
Hard times in the Northern Mariana Islands are detailed in GAO-07-746T, testimony from April 19, 2007. The commonwealth governs itself under its own constitution. It spans 14 islands in the North Pacific. Its land area is about 2.5 times that of Washington, D.C. GAO's statement rests on a December 2006 report on U.S. insular areas. It adds audited data through fiscal year 2005 and fresh fiscal year 2006 facts.

The islands' economy shrank as key industries faded. The government's main fund fell into deficit in fiscal year 2002. It kept sliding through fiscal year 2005. Debt grew as spending topped revenue year after year. In fiscal year 2006, leaders imposed furlough days and other harsh cuts. Weak audits and poor financial data made the crisis hard to track. GAO backed Interior Department efforts to lift the economy. It also pressed for sound books and full audits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-806t:
Cleanup of homes near the World Trade Center is covered in GAO-07-806T, testimony from June 20, 2007. Dust from the September 11 attacks coated Lower Manhattan in asbestos, lead, and glass fibers. The Environmental Protection Agency ran a first indoor clean-and-test program in 2002 and 2003. In December 2006, it announced a second program. Work was set to start later in 2007. GAO gave early views on how the agency built that plan.

An expert panel and the agency's inspector general had urged changes after the first round. GAO checked how far the agency followed their advice. It also judged what the new plan tells the public. Early gaps in the facts given to residents drew concern. GAO also weighed whether the agency has the funds and staff for the work. The statement is based on a review still under way. Final findings were to come later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-826t:
Dental care for children on Medicaid is the topic of GAO-07-826T, testimony dated May 2, 2007. Medicaid covers 31 million children. Tooth decay is common among them and can turn deadly if ignored. Federal law grants these children a broad health benefit that includes dental care. The Medicare and Medicaid agency oversees the benefit. States run the programs and report service data. GAO drew on its reports from 2000 through 2003. It refreshed that work with talks in April 2007.

Concerns about the data remain, GAO said. State reports do not show well how many children truly get dental care. Weak data blind the federal agency to gaps in service. States vary in how fully they report the required figures. GAO spoke with officials in five states for the update. Without sound counts, Congress cannot tell if the dental benefit works. The statement urges attention to the data problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-856t:
Drug safety calls at the Food and Drug Administration fill GAO-07-856T, testimony dated May 9, 2007. In 2004, several big drug safety cases shook public trust. In some, staff inside the agency disagreed on how to act. GAO's March 2006 report studied how the agency decides such cases. Two offices share the work. The Office of New Drugs approves new drugs and tracks their safety. The Office of Drug Safety focuses on risks after drugs reach the market.

The two offices' roles blur in hard cases, GAO found. Decision steps lack a clear record of who decided what, and why. Case studies of four drugs showed the strain: Arava, Baycol, Bextra, and Propulsid. The safety office is now called the Office of Surveillance and Epidemiology. GAO checked steps the agency took since March 2006 to improve. Its testimony updates Congress on that progress. Clearer decision rights remain the core need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-896t:
The ban on taxes for Internet access is explained in GAO-07-896T, testimony dated May 23, 2007. About 92 million U.S. adults used the Internet on a typical day at the end of 2006. Congress barred new state and local taxes on access in 1998. Older taxes were allowed to stay. A 2004 update told GAO to study the ban's effect on revenues. This statement rests on GAO's 2006 report on the topic. It makes no recommendations.

The ban covers what providers reasonably bundle for users, GAO reads the law to say. That includes email and DSL service sold with access. It does not cover the wholesale capacity that providers buy to deliver access. Some states and firms read the line differently. Revenue effects vary widely by state, the study found. States with grandfathered taxes face the largest stakes. The testimony frames the choices as Congress weighs the ban's future.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-926t:
Colleges serving poor and minority students get an update in GAO-07-926T, testimony dated June 4, 2007. Federal grants under two titles reached $448 million in fiscal year 2006. Over 500 schools shared the money. Recipients include Black colleges, tribal colleges, and Hispanic-serving schools. Funding nearly doubled since fiscal year 1999. Schools use grants to lift teaching quality and student support. One tribal college funded distance learning with its grant. GAO checked how the Education Department watches the programs.

Oversight has improved since GAO's 2004 report, the statement says. The department changed how it monitors grantees and helps them. Performance reports show wide-ranging benefits at schools. Management systems and student services both gained. More progress is still needed, GAO found. Goals and strategies for the programs remain thin in places. Site help and data checks need strengthening. The testimony updates Congress on the remaining gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1016t:
State oversight of long-term care insurance fills GAO testimony GAO-08-1016T of July 24, 2008. As the baby boom generation ages, demand for long-term care will grow. Private insurance could ease the load on state and federal budgets. States hold the main duty of watching this market. Buyers have faced sharp premium rises and denied claims.

The testimony rests on a GAO report issued in June 2008. It reviews how states police rate setting by insurers. It also reviews how states handle claims settlement practices. GAO gathered data from all states and studied 10 states in depth. The statement shows where consumer protection is strong and where it lags.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1026t:
Lessons on managing for results fill GAO testimony GAO-08-1026T of July 24, 2008. For 15 years, reforms have tried to shift federal management from counting activities to weighing outcomes. GAO found that agencies now have a solid base of strategic plans, measures, and reports. That base can help programs improve.

Yet GAO also found less progress in a key area. Managers still make too little use of performance data in their choices. The testimony draws on GAO surveys of managers run in 1997, 2000, 2003, and 2007. It offers ways agencies can spur wider use of such data. It closes with lessons from past reforms for the next administration.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1056t:
Purchasing controls at veterans' hospitals are probed in GAO testimony GAO-08-1056T, given on July 31, 2008. The Veterans Health Administration has used miscellaneous obligations for over 60 years. These entries record estimated sums owed for later purchases. In fiscal year 2007, a large share of its buying ran through them. That scale raised doubts about control over billions of dollars.

The testimony shares early findings from GAO's audit. GAO tested a sample of 42 such entries at three sites. It checked how the entries were used and whether agency rules guard their approval. A draft report holds four recommendations to tighten controls. A final report was set to follow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1126t:
Training of veterans' claims staff is examined in GAO testimony GAO-08-1126T (September 18, 2008). The disability claims process has long drawn concern for slow decisions and large backlogs. The Department of Veterans Affairs has hired almost 3,000 new claims processors since January 2007. Good training decides whether that hiring surge pays off.

The testimony rests on a GAO report from May 2008. It reviews how the agency trains new and seasoned processors. It also reviews how managers judge their work. Sound performance management helps staff issue decisions that are timely, accurate, and consistent. GAO found that both systems need improvement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1136t:
Airline checks of passengers against watch lists are reviewed in GAO testimony GAO-08-1136T of September 9, 2008. Domestic airlines must match passenger names against terrorist watch-list records. Matches can bar a person from flying or trigger extra screening. The Transportation Security Administration is set to take over this task through its Secure Flight program. Delays have left airlines in the role.

The testimony sets out the rules airlines must follow. It weighs how far the agency has checked airline compliance. It also tracks progress on Secure Flight. GAO found oversight growing stronger. Still, the agency expects the lasting fix to be its own program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1146t:
Military sexual assault programs get a full review in GAO statement GAO-08-1146T, dated September 10, 2008. In 2004, Congress told the Defense Department to build a full policy on assaults involving servicemembers. The Coast Guard set up a like program on its own. The statement rests on GAO's report issued August 29, 2008.

GAO checked how far both services have put their programs in place. It weighed how well they track assault reports and watch over cases. More than 3,900 servicemembers shared their views through surveys and talks. GAO made 11 recommendations. They call for stronger guidance, training, and oversight across both programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1156t:
Diversity gains inside GAO itself are reviewed in GAO testimony GAO-08-1156T of September 16, 2008. The agency employs about 3,100 staff in Washington and 11 field offices. More than half hold advanced degrees. A 1980 law gave GAO its own personnel system. In 2001, it set up an office to lead work on fairness and inclusion.

The testimony weighs diversity among senior executives and managers. Gains have been made over the past decade. Still, the title warns that sustained attention is needed to build on them. The statement shows how the watchdog agency applies its own standards to its workforce.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1166t:
Harmful exports of used electronics are revisited in GAO testimony GAO-08-1166T, presented September 17, 2008. More consumers now recycle old devices to avoid the harm of dumping them. Some firms instead ship the gear to developing countries. Unsafe recycling there can damage health and the environment. Screen tubes are a special risk because they hold lead.

The testimony rests on GAO's report from August 2008. GAO tracked where exported devices end up. It tested the rules that govern such exports and weighed stronger options. Its title gives the verdict: exports flow almost unchecked, due to thin enforcement and narrow rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-126t:
Port security one year after a new law is surveyed in GAO testimony GAO-08-126T of October 30, 2007. The nation's 361 seaports anchor both safety and trade. The SAFE Port Act rewrote parts of maritime law and set up new programs. Homeland security bodies share the work, led by the Coast Guard and two sister agencies.

The testimony blends finished GAO work with early findings from current reviews. It covers port security as a whole. It then looks at security at single facilities and at cargo containers. GAO staff visited ports at home and abroad. The statement gives Congress a status check on the law's rollout.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-146t:
Abuse claims at youth treatment programs are investigated in GAO testimony GAO-08-146T, presented October 10, 2007. These programs serve troubled boys and girls across the country. They offer drug treatment, counseling, and military-style discipline. Some call themselves wilderness therapy or boot camps. Many report good results. Claims of abuse and death shadow others.

A House committee asked GAO to test how widespread the claims are. GAO also probed closed cases in which a teenager died at a private program. It read police and autopsy records and state reviews, some dating back to 1990. The testimony reports what those records show.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-186t:
New crewed spacecraft risks are laid out in GAO testimony GAO-08-186T, given on April 3, 2008. NASA is building the Ares I rocket and the Orion crew vehicle. They must return humans to flight after the Shuttle retires in 2010. A launch is planned for 2015, leaving a 5-year gap. Past GAO work has questioned the cost and buying plans for both craft.

NASA has already changed course on parts of the work after GAO's advice. The testimony sets out the types of hurdles the projects face. It also names key signs that leaders can watch to judge risk. Those signs target the trouble spots that often sink such builds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-216t:
Aircraft noise and airport growth collide in GAO testimony dated October 24, 2007, filed as GAO-08-216T. Planners expect air traffic to rise. A new traffic system would add runways and reshape flight paths. Community anger over noise is a major block to that growth. The planning office calls noise a primary constraint on the new system.

The testimony sets out what drives a community's exposure to aircraft noise. It reviews the state of efforts to cut or soften that noise. It then names the chief hurdles and next steps. GAO drew on past work, including a survey of the 50 largest airports, plus fresh data and talks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-226t:
Small business loan guarantees are measured in GAO testimony GAO-08-226T, presented November 1, 2007. The 7(a) program began in 1953. It backs loans for firms that cannot get credit on the open market. In fiscal year 2006, it helped more than 80,000 businesses. Its guarantees came to nearly $14 billion.

The testimony rests on a GAO report from 2007. It sets out the program's purpose and the yardsticks used to judge it. It weighs proof of credit barriers facing small firms. It also maps which market segments the program serves beside bank loans. Subsidy costs and the doubts around them close the account. GAO's verdict: more performance measures are needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-246t:
United Nations reform is surveyed in GAO testimony GAO-08-246T, presented January 24, 2008. Long-running flaws in UN management drive calls to modernize the body. The United States has pressed hard for such reform. The testimony rests on recent GAO reports. It spans both headquarters practice and field work in one troubled nation.

First, it reviews reform steps at the UN Secretariat since 2006. Next, it weighs oversight and accountability in chosen UN bodies. Last, it turns to Burma, where the ruling junta has curbed the work of global aid groups for 3 years. The statement shows where reform has moved and where it stalls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-286t:
GAO's own undercover methods are explained in testimony GAO-08-286T of November 14, 2007. A special investigations unit was formed in 2005. Its mixed team of investigators, auditors, and analysts runs covert tests for Congress. The tests hunt for weak controls that could endanger security, public safety, or tax dollars. Agencies get no warning before a test.

Fresh concern drives this statement. Reports claimed that airport security chiefs may have leaked word of coming tests to screeners. That would spoil the results. GAO sets out how its red team work is run and guarded. It gives examples of past covert operations to show the method's worth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-436t:
With its testimony GAO-08-436T, presented on January 24, 2008, GAO turns to contractor support for deployed forces. Contractors feed, house, and back troops in the field; some 129,000 were sent to Iraq. No single official made that call, which GAO says fed years of oversight problems.

The Defense Department issued full guidance on contractor support in 2005, but GAO found little proof that units follow it. Old problems persist: planning steps are skipped, oversight staff are too few, lessons are not gathered, and training for overseers and commanders is thin. Poor oversight has cost money and hurt operations. Ahead, the department must fit contractors into its total force plans and settle the right mix of contractors and troops. The statement lists steps Congress may wish to require.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-456t:
Aviation security planning at the Transportation Security Administration is the focus of GAO testimony GAO-08-456T, presented on February 28, 2008. Funding for aviation security has totaled about $26 billion since fiscal year 2004. The statement covers passenger screening, air cargo, and the Secure Flight watch-list matching program.

The agency has sharpened how it deploys screeners, tightened screening steps, and worked on better screening technology. Air cargo security has also been strengthened. GAO credits risk management as a stated cornerstone of agency policy, now built into several efforts. Hard choices remain as threats shift and funds stay finite. GAO urges fuller use of risk management in planning and watching these programs, so money flows to the areas of greatest need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-476t:
The Federal Protective Service is sized up in GAO testimony GAO-08-476T, presented on February 8, 2008. The service guards about 8,800 federal facilities owned or leased by the General Services Administration. It fields about 1,100 staff and about 15,000 contract guards.

Staffing and operational strains keep the service from fully meeting its mission, GAO found. Its workforce fell by nearly 20 percent, from almost 1,400 in fiscal year 2004 to about 1,100 at the end of fiscal year 2007. A shift to inspectors over police officers has ended proactive patrols at most sites. Hours have been cut, and gear such as cameras and x-ray machines is not always kept up. Budget strain and thin planning add to the problem. Full findings and any recommendations were promised in later work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-496t:
Federal information security comes up in GAO testimony GAO-08-496T, presented on February 14, 2008. GAO has called this area high risk in every biennial report since 1997. The Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002 sets the duties agencies must meet each year.

Reported scores keep rising. Certified and accredited systems climbed from 88 percent to 92 percent, control testing from 88 percent to 95 percent, and contingency plan testing from 77 percent to 86 percent. Yet audits still find deep flaws at most big agencies. Access controls leak, patches lag, duties are not split safely, and backup plans are incomplete. The root cause, GAO says, is that agencywide security programs are still not fully in place, leaving federal data open to misuse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-506t:
Missile defense work is summed up in GAO testimony GAO-08-506T, presented on February 26, 2008. The Missile Defense Agency's system is the Defense Department's largest research effort, at $8 billion to $10 billion a year. The statement gives the same Block 2006 review as GAO's March 2008 report to Congress.

The agency fielded new and upgraded assets in the past year and met most test goals. It still fell short of its block targets: fewer assets fielded, costs up by about $1 billion, and fewer tests flown. Deferred work hides the block's true cost, and some contractors overran their fiscal year 2007 budgets. Too few realistic flight tests exist to prove how the whole system would fight. Oversight has tightened lately under a new missile defense board.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-556t:
Energy research funding comes up in GAO testimony GAO-08-556T, presented on March 5, 2008. The Energy Department has long funded work on renewable, fossil, and nuclear power, plus basic science. High prices and emission worries have renewed interest in advanced energy technology.

Inflation-adjusted funding for energy research fell 92 percent from a $6 billion peak in fiscal year 1978 to $505 million in fiscal year 1998. It has since climbed back to $1.4 billion in fiscal year 2008. The fiscal year 2009 request seeks 34 percent more for fossil work and 44 percent more for nuclear work, plus $4.7 billion for basic science. After $57.5 billion spent over 30 years, fossil fuels still supply 85 percent of national energy. Cost and emissions remain the core hurdles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-616t:
GAO speaks for its own budget in GAO-08-616T, testimony dated April 10, 2008. The office asked Congress for $545.5 million for fiscal year 2009, a rise of 7.5 percent. The statement explains what the money would buy and what taxpayers got from past funding.

In fiscal year 2007, GAO says its work brought $45.9 billion in money gains, or $94 back for each dollar spent. It also led to more than 1,300 fixes in how agencies run, and its staff spoke at 276 hearings. Demand keeps climbing, with more than 1,200 study requests in one year. The testimony makes the case that oversight pays for itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-636t:
After the September 11 attacks, states and cities built fusion centers where agencies share tips on crime and terror plots. GAO-08-636T, testimony dated April 17, 2008, describes the 58 centers GAO studied and how federal agencies help them. The testimony rests on an October 2007 report.

Most centers take a broad mission that covers both terror threats and regular law work. State police lead most of them, and federal staff sat in most working centers by September 2007. Federal agencies gave access to their data systems and granted security clearances. Center staff still struggled with too many systems at once. GAO urged a clear long-term federal role.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-646t:
Merging many agencies into the Department of Homeland Security in March 2003 was a huge management task. GAO-08-646T, testimony dated April 9, 2008, grades the department's core management work: buying, money, staff, computers, and property. Big mergers can take 5 to 7 years to settle, GAO notes.

Each area shows gains mixed with gaps. Buying outcomes lack clear ownership, and oversight of some contractor work is thin. Auditors still could not give the books a clean pass for fiscal year 2007. Staff systems are not yet tied to the department's strategy. GAO notes it has made more than 900 fix proposals to the department in 5 years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-686t:
Humane slaughter law says farm animals must be handled and killed without needless pain. More than 150 million animals were slaughtered for food in fiscal year 2007. GAO-08-686T, testimony dated April 17, 2008, revisits GAO's 2004 report on how the Agriculture Department enforces that law.

Inspection records were patchy and uneven in 2004, so no one could say how often abuse happened. Plant shutdown calls for grave or repeat abuse lacked steady rules. Congress wants yearly public reports on violations, but the last one came in March 2003 and used weak data. Open reporting, GAO says, would expose enforcement gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-696t:
More than 200,000 youth lived in care facilities with federal aid in 2004. Some sites were linked to abuse and even deaths. GAO-08-696T, testimony dated April 24, 2008, shares early survey results from state agencies on harm to youth in such homes and on state oversight.

Survey replies came from 49 states on probes of abuse claims in 2006. A full 28 states reported deaths. No pattern tied harm to one kind of site. Some sites skip state licensing, and rules miss risks like suicide. Yearly visits fall short when staff run thin. Federal agencies also lack clean data to hold states to account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-706t:
Plane travel keeps growing, and so does the pollution from planes and airports. GAO-08-706T, testimony dated May 6, 2008, looks at two paths to cut that harm: a new air traffic system called NextGen, and long-term research on cleaner planes and engines.

Aviation makes less than 1 percent of local air pollution and about 2.7 percent of U.S. greenhouse gases, by federal counts. Those shares will grow with traffic. Straighter flight paths under NextGen could save fuel soon. Past research has already cut plane emissions a lot through better engines. The testimony weighs near wins against slower research gains.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-726t:
A giant oil stockpile guards the economy against supply shocks. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve, built in 1975, holds about 700 million barrels. Law from 2005 orders growth to 1 billion barrels by 2018. GAO-08-726T, testimony dated April 24, 2008, shares cheaper ways to fill it.

Mixing in heavy crude could save over $1 billion on a 100 million barrel buy, given a $12 price gap with light crude. Heavy oil also fits many Gulf Coast plants better. Buying a set dollar sum over time, rather than a set volume, would grab more oil when prices dip. The energy department was weighing both ideas.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-776t:
Security clearances decide who may see the nation's secrets, and backlogs have plagued the process for years. Defense handles 80 percent of federal clearances. GAO-08-776T, testimony dated May 22, 2008, distills lessons from GAO work since 1974 on how to reform the system.

Four factors stand out. Agencies must ask only for the clearance a job truly needs; a top secret held 10 years costs about 30 times a secret one. Quality must be built into each step. Leaders need full measures of speed and quality, not just one side. And reform needs steady long-term funding, not year-to-year scraps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-886t:
Paper forms are back at the center of the 2010 census. On April 3, 2008, the Commerce chief scrapped handheld computers for home visits to non-responders. GAO-08-886T, testimony dated June 11, 2008, reviews the new paper plan, the tech contract, and the master schedule.

A May 8, 2008 plan spells out the paper operation and how it will be run. But the computer system that steers field work had flopped in dress rehearsal tests. Fresh tactics, like second mailings, will not get a full rehearsal either. That leaves their effect on the 2010 count hard to guess. GAO makes no new calls at this time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-916t:
The 2008 economic stimulus flooded the Internal Revenue Service with phone calls. GAO-08-916T, June 2008 testimony, reports data on what the surge did to IRS phone service and costs. Millions of people who normally do not file returns had to file to claim a payment, and payment amounts and timing varied by household. GAO drew on its filing season monitoring at the subcommittee's request.

Demand was unprecedented, IRS said. In the week ending May 24, call volume ran almost six times the same week a year earlier. Even after staff were pulled from collections work, only 39 percent of callers seeking an assistor got through, down from 80 percent a year before. Running the program could cost up to $862 million; IRS had received a $202 million supplemental appropriation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-926t:
For the 11th straight year, GAO could not sign off on the U.S. government's own books. GAO-08-926T, June 2008 testimony, presents the fiscal year 2007 audit results. Lawmakers need sound money data to steer programs and policy, but weak controls again blocked a clean opinion on the combined statements. One part did pass: the 2007 Statement of Social Insurance earned a clean opinion.

Three problems keep recurring. The Defense Department has deep flaws in how it tracks its money. Agencies cannot match and settle the transfers they make between each other. And the process for building the government-wide statements is weak. Progress is real, though. Many agency audits have improved, and the government issued its first summary report for a wider audience. GAO ties steady gains here to facing the long-term fiscal challenge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-96t:
Port inspectors who check farm goods at U.S. ports of entry are the subject of GAO-08-96T, a testimony given on October 3, 2007. Farm trade brings in over $1 trillion a year, yet pests and plant diseases can ride in with cargo and travelers. The work moved from the Agriculture Department to Customs and Border Protection in March 2003.

GAO reports that the two agencies added training, shared targeting tools, and set up joint reviews of ports. Still, a survey of farm inspectors found many doing fewer checks than before. Most said the farm mission got less weight inside the larger agency. GAO points to weak measures of results, thin training, and short supplies as risks to fix.
